title: Collective-State Preparation in a Subwavelength Triangular Trimer Using SUPER Excitation
authors: Thomas Nunner, Johannes Kerber, Helmut Ritsch, Arpita Pal
abstract: The Swing-UP of quantum EmitteR population (SUPER) scheme has recently been proposed as a deterministic method for the preparation of collective radiative states in two strongly dipole-coupled quantum emitters (Phys. Rev. Res. \textbf{8}, 013179 (2026)). Here, we extend this approach to an equilateral subwavelength triangular trimer of dipole-coupled two-level quantum emitters (QEs), loosely inspired by biological light-harvesting ring geometries. Using tailored, time-overlapping, red-detuned ultrashort SUPER pulses, we numerically investigate the selective preparation of collective target states. We find that both the state selectivity and the preparation efficiency depend strongly on the inter-emitter spacing. In particular, at deep-subwavelength separations, the symmetric collective state can be deterministically prepared with near-unity efficiency, whereas the inversion efficiency and state selectivity are significantly lower at larger inter-emitter separations. Furthermore, this state preparation technique inherits a certain degree of robustness against reasonable static position imperfections and on-site frequency inhomogeneities of the individual QEs. Our results demonstrate that deep-subwavelength triangular trimers and, more broadly, highly compact ring geometries are excellent candidates for the deterministic preparation of collective radiative states via SUPER excitation. These predictions could be realized with solid-state emitters and molecules. Our findings offer a route toward the direct probing of the `pure' electromagnetic layer of interaction in biological and bio-inspired synthetic nanophotonic ring configurations, with possible relevance in photonics, quantum information processing, and metrology.
summary: The paper demonstrates a method using SUPER excitation pulses to deterministically prepare specific collective quantum states in a triangular array of three coupled quantum emitters. The efficiency is critically dependent on the emitter spacing, showing near-perfect control only when the emitters are placed at deep-subwavelength separations. This work suggests that highly compact nanostructures are excellent platforms for controlling collective quantum phenomena.
main_problem: The goal is the deterministic preparation of specific collective radiative states within a nanoscale array of quantum emitters.
main_result: Near-unity efficiency for preparing the symmetric collective state is achieved when the emitter spacing is deep-subwavelength, demonstrating that compact geometries are highly favorable for this control scheme.
method: The study uses numerical simulation solving the Lindblad master equation under the influence of tailored, time-overlapping, red-detuned ultrashort excitation pulses (SUPER).
model_or_system: The system is modeled as an equilateral triangular trimer of three dipole-coupled two-level quantum emitters, inspired by biological light-harvesting structures. The dynamics are governed by the full Hamiltonian and a Lindblad master equation.
key_observables: State selectivity, preparation efficiency (population inversion) into specific collective states like $|S_1\rangle$.
important_parameters: Inter-emitter spacing ($d$), which is critical; deep-subwavelength separations ($d \ll 0.01\lambda_0$) are optimal.
main_assumptions: The model relies on the coupled-dipole approximation and assumes weak system-environment interaction, though robustness against minor disorder is shown.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of population inversion into the symmetric state $|S_1\rangle$, showing high fidelity at small separations ($d = 0.01\lambda_0$) compared to significantly lower efficiency at larger separations ($d = 0.1\lambda_0$).
paper_structure: The paper extends the SUPER excitation scheme from two emitters to a trimer, numerically investigating how state selectivity and preparation efficiency depend on inter-emitter spacing by solving the master equation with tailored pulses.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum control in engineered nanoscale light-matter interactions, providing concrete theoretical predictions for achieving high-fidelity collective state preparation relevant to solid-state emitters and bio-inspired photonics.
